relations.note: Guevara conjectures Anchimalhuén as the Moon or woman of the Sun, later described as Antü's wife.
Modern accounts say Anchimallén's ember-like or meteor-like form may be mistaken for Cherufe.
Neuquén testimony assigns both beings similar purposes and flying nocturnal forms, without narrating a meeting.
Anchimalguén apparitions appear in a cave alongside imbunches; no further relationship is stated.
Some regional accounts describe witches dispatching this luminous nocturnal being.
Guevara speculates Anchimalhuén represented the Moon, ordinarily called Küyen; later works conflate or separate them.
Sun and Moon jointly create or care for the primordial world.
Antü and Küyen are husband and wife in regional Neuquén traditions.
Küyen is Antü’s wife in regional Puelmapu traditions.
Küyen and Antü marry where Earth ends but repeatedly fail to meet.

relations.myth: Troubled marriage of Antü and Küyen
relations.note: Antü strikes Küyen, whose marked face recalls the marital violence.
Antü pursues his retreating wife across the sky but cannot catch her.
After their separation, Antü eternally pursues Küyen but cannot catch her.
Antü strikes Küyen, staining her face and bruising one eye.
They alternate illumination and care for dispersed human beings.
Küyen and Antü alternately illuminate Earth and care for humanity.
Sun and Moon jointly create or oversee beings before the serpent conflict.
Küyen quarrels with Antü and weeps when he takes a celestial maiden.
Some accounts identify or incorporate Antü's solar-lunar family within fourfold Ngünechen.
Modern syntheses identify Antü as the chief or solar Pillan.
Some late accounts identify the sea ruler as the vessel’s creator.
Some late retellings say Millalobo created the supernatural vessel.

relations.myth: Millalobo governs access to the Caleuche
relations.note: Some late accounts make Millalobo its maritime superior and rule-giver.
Alternative retellings make Millalobo the ship's owner or controlling authority.
Contested later retellings say Pincoya guides drowned sailors to the ghost ship Caleuche.

relations.myth: Pincoya delivers drowned mariners to the Caleuche
relations.note: Pincoya conveys drowned bodies aboard, where the ship revives them.

relations.myth: Pincoy helps carry the drowned aboard
relations.note: Pincoy assists Pincoya in transporting drowned mariners to the vessel.
Ranquel narrator Macedonio Carripí identifies Cherufe as Ngenechén.
After Cheburbue counsels Caupolicán, he offers tobacco incense to Pillán.
A harmful sorcerer travels as the Chonchón or projects the flying head.
A powerful witch may transform into, project, or travel as this flying head or night bird.
Modern hierarchical accounts place Cuero under Millalobo's authority without a discrete episode.
Some authors conflate their similar aquatic forms and behavior, though Guevara distinguishes them.
The hide-shaped form is sometimes conflated with Cuero, though Guevara distinguishes them.
Modern analysis associates Cuero’s hide form with Shumpall water-personification and groups it under nwenko.
Some informants identify Cuero as the aquatic bodily form assumed by a harmful Wekufü.
Chilote witches allegedly deform a stolen or surrendered infant into the cave-dwelling Invunche.

relations.myth: Invunche guards and advises the witches
relations.note: The Invunche allegedly guards the witches’ cave, advises them, and serves as an instrument of vengeance.
The catastrophe grounds survivors’ renewed relationship with Chau Ngünechen and the ngillatun.

relations.myth: Flood survivors become the first Sumpall
relations.note: Popular retellings claim Trentren helped transform flood victims into Sumpall; this derives from modern comparative reconstruction.
Later interpreters structurally relate Tren-Tren’s transformed aquatic survivors to the Sumpall cycle.

relations.myth: Filew counters harmful forces sent through kalku sorcery
relations.note: Filew empowers diagnosis and resistance against attacks attributed to a kalku.
Kalku allegedly direct, bargain with, or exploit harmful forces against victims.
Variable accounts merge Küyen, Antü, the divine family, and the creator.
A modern retelling says Ngenechen presides over Küyen’s marriage to Antü.

relations.myth: Ngen selects machi and delegates power through Filew
relations.note: Regional testimony links tutelary ngen with Filew in selecting and empowering practitioners.

relations.myth: Filew and Ngünechen merge in some practitioners’ accounts
relations.note: Recent ritual testimony sometimes identifies Filew with Ngünechen and sometimes distinguishes them.

relations.myth: Unity of the four divine persons
relations.note: Filew is described as Ngünechen's spirit and the unifying principle of four persons.

relations.myth: Ngünechen sends Filew to sustain the succession of machi
relations.note: Filew acts as Ngünechen’s Spirit of Power and Wisdom.
Filew positively possesses the prospective machi; Wekufe negatively possesses the patient.
relations.source: Foerster, Introducción a la religiosidad mapuche

relations.note: Modern Chiloé analysis sometimes interprets Millalobo as a maritime ngen.
Modern hierarchical accounts place Piuchén under Millalobo's authority without a discrete episode.
Millalobo delegates fish and shellfish abundance and distribution to Pincoya.

relations.myth: Huenchula and the birth of Pincoya
relations.note: Later tradition makes Pincoya the daughter of Millalobo and Huenchula.
Late genealogies identify Pincoy as Millalobo's son.
Pincoya becomes a subordinate helper or princess within Millalobo’s marine kingdom.
Some modern formulations make Ngünechen creator or superior of nature owners.
Other explanations treat Ngen as localized expressions or an aggregate of Ngünechen's power.
Popular accounts place the ngen’s institution after destructive pillan conflict.
Contemporary Chiloé testimony identifies Pincoya as an owner of shellfish and intertidal abundance.
Scholars proposed that Ngünechen partially absorbed Pillán's atmospheric and sovereign functions.

relations.myth: Cosmological opposition of life and destruction
relations.note: Later systems contrast life-giving Ngünechen with destructive Wekufe without narrating personal combat.
A Botxolwe community publication overlaps this local aquatic divinity with Augusta’s definition of Shompallwe.
Nahuelpi said a Wekufe could appear in a comparable whirlwind form.
Pillan's rain assists Trauco and Kai-Kai in flooding the world.

relations.myth: Huecubuyes consult Pillán in secluded caves
relations.note: Disputed huecubuye specialists consult Pillán; their connection with Wekufe is uncertain.
Later syntheses describe Huecubu as dependent upon or controlled by Pillán.

relations.myth: Joint invocation in sickness and necessity
relations.note: Elders and ritual specialists advised invoking Pillan and Wekufü together.
relations.source: Valdivia, Sermón en lengua de Chile

relations.myth: Alternative causes of volcanic smoke, ash, and stones
relations.note: Pillán or Wekufü is credited with causing destructive volcanic emissions.
relations.source: Coña and Moesbach, Vida y costumbres

relations.myth: Aquatic abduction contrasted with predatory hide attack
relations.note: Comparative analysis contrasts Sumpall's marital abduction with Trülke Wekufü's destructive attack.

Alwe.myth: Capture of a recently dead person's soul
Alwe.note: Uncertain later summaries say a wekufe may capture and employ a dead person's soul.

Armadillo.note: Elal takes fire after Armadillo and the other animal owners conceal it.
Elal slashes Armadillo’s shell, explaining its permanent markings.

Basilisco chilote.note: Later collectors compare or conflate Colo Colo with the Chilote basilisk tradition.

Basilisk of Chiloé.myth: The transformed rooster lays the Basilisk’s egg
Basilisk of Chiloé.note: The red rooster lays the Basilisk’s egg, then becomes a Piguchén.
Basilisk of Chiloé.source: Cavada, Chiloé y los chilotes, p. 109

Caballo Marino.myth: Brujos ride the sea-horse to board the Caleuche
Caballo Marino.note: The sea-horse transports brujos to the vessel, carrying as many as twelve.
Recent compendia place the sea horses under Millalobo's rule and protection.

Cahuel.note: Grouped dolphins indicate pursuit by the Caleuche; later lore personifies its herald.

Caicai-Vilu.note: Caicai approves Millalobo and appoints him lord and representative over the seas.

Chaw Antü.note: Chaw Antü corresponds to Ngünechen's elder male heavenly aspect in some Huilliche schemes.

Chibato.note: Chibato and Ibunche emerge together as distinct, disfigured cave captives.
Chibato.source: Mateo Coñuecar deposition, Proceso de los brujos de Chiloé

Chilote Sirena.note: Later standardized genealogy makes Pincoya and the Chilote Sirena sisters.

Chilote Sirena.myth: Complementary guardians of shore and sea
Chilote Sirena.note: Pincoya guards shellfish while Sirena guards fish, assigning them complementary maritime domains.
Chilote Sirena.source: Rosa Chiguay testimony, cited by Núñez

Chilote Sirena.note: Later retellings make Pincoya and Sirena jointly carry drowned sailors to the Caleuche.

Chivato Pillán.note: Anchimalguén guards a cave that also contains a Chivato Pillán.

Christian God.note: Some Selk’nam speakers equated or compared Temáukel with the Christian God.

Condor.note: After Condor refuses a feather and insults him, Elal shoots him down.
Elal plucks Condor’s head and decrees that it will remain permanently bald.
Elal takes feathers from the wounded Condor for use on his arrows.

Cuchivilu.note: Modern hierarchical accounts place Cuchivilu under Millalobo's authority without a discrete episode.
Later Chiloé compendia sometimes merge their names despite distinct morphologies.

Dangerous Rhea egg.note: Elal destroys the magically lethal egg with an arrow to obtain the required item.

Daughter of Sun.note: In Hughes’s version Elal marries Sun and Moon’s daughter.
Elal seeks her as bride but detects her parents’ substitution and leaves unmarried.
Some variants say Elal completes the trials but rejects the daughter after discovering deception.

Elchen.note: Popular modern summaries make Elchen Antü's collaborator or subordinate creator.

Elmapu.note: Popular modern summaries make Elmapu Antü's collaborator or subordinate creator.

Elmapun.note: The maker or placer of the land was consolidated into Ngünechen's creator attributes.

Fiura.note: Early sources record Fiura as an alternative name for the Trauco.
Later Chilote literature makes Fiura his wife or female partner.
Late genealogies make Fiura his daughter as well as his wife.

Fox.note: Fox submits to Elal’s authority and accompanies him on his journeys.

Füta Chachai.note: With Ñuke Papai, makes the world and appoints ngen as caretakers.

Goshge.note: Elal becomes a horsefly, enters the child-eating giant, and stings him to death.
Elal changes Góos’s legs into fins and sends the terrestrial whale to sea.

Güenupillán.note: Plural guecubus are subordinate chiefs commanded by Güenupillán.

Huenchula.myth: Huenchula and the birth of Pincoya
Huenchula.note: Huenchula becomes Millalobo's wife and lives with him beneath the sea.

Huenchula.myth: Huenchula and the birth of Pincoya
Huenchula.note: Some versions say Millalobo seduces Huenchula and leads her beneath the water.
Other versions characterize Millalobo's taking of Huenchula as an abduction.
Later genealogy identifies the human Huenchula as Pincoya’s mother.
Blume’s structural analysis classifies Pincoya as subordinate helper or servant to Huenchula.

Huenchur.myth: Huenchur orders Cahuelche to announce the Caleuche
Huenchur.note: Huenchur commands the Cahuelche whose leaps herald the vessel.

Jesus.note: A machi describes Mary, Moon, and Jesus as inseparable.
Jesus.source: Bacigalupo, Shamans of the Foye Tree

Jesus Christ.note: Scripture and catechisms present Christ as son of the God translated Ngünechen.

Kai-Kai.note: Tren-Tren commands survivors to offer a quartered child partly to Kai-Kai.
Kai-Kai.source: Rosales, Historia general, book I, chapter 1

Kai-Kai.note: Recent Chiloé scholarship classifies Kai-Kai among maritime ngen.
Pillan produces catastrophic rain that assists Kai-Kai's inundation.

Kaikai.note: Modern retellings oppose Ngünechen's protection to the destructive waters raised by Kaikai.

Kallfümalen.note: Late regional discussions align female Sumpall with the Blue Maiden, without narrating them as separate interacting beings.

Kay Kay.note: The destructive flood serpent is subordinate to Küyen and Antü.

Kaykay.note: Antü and Küyen precede Kaykay's flood struggle in some Neuquén accounts.

Kénos.myth: Commissioning Kénos to order the primordial earth
Kénos.note: Temáukel sends Kénos to order earth, establish norms, and form humanity.

Kóoch.note: Kóoch creates the primordial cosmos before Elal makes the human world inhabitable.

La Condená.note: Late genealogy says he couples with La Condená and fathers Fiura.

Laftrache.note: Comparative folklore likens their small humanoid forms, but records no shared episode or kinship.

Mankián.myth: Women travelling alone at dangerous hours
Mankián.note: Anchimallén and Mankián jointly appear in Norma Huentén's modern admonitory narrative.

Mocho-Choshuenco’s spirit.note: Rukapillan defeats the hostile volcano spirit after it spreads illness.
Rukapillan's thunderbolt truncates its crater and leaves the volcano inactive.

Ngen-ko.note: Quillén testimony classifies Guirivilu beings as water owners.

Ngen-mawida.note: Modern interpretation sometimes treats the Trauco as a transformed Williche forest ngen.

Ngenemapun.note: The land's governor or sustainer is paired or merged with Ngünechen.

Ngen’ko.note: Contemporary father-water etymology equates Chawko with an ngen’ko, though Núñez rejects it.

Ngürüvilu.note: Twentieth-century compilations sometimes classify this water creature as a wekufe usable by kalku.

Nóshtex.note: Nóshtex is Elal’s father in the earliest recorded genealogy.
Elal temporarily submits to Nóshtex, then escapes his pursuit behind a raised forest.
Nóshtex extracts Elal from his murdered mother and intends to eat him.

Pampas Cat.note: Elal takes fire concealed by Pampas Cat and the other animal owners.
Elal punishes Pampas Cat less severely than Armadillo and Skunk.

Peripillán.note: A modern reconstruction makes Peripillán leader of a celestial rebellion against Antü.
Antü defeats and buries Peripillán beneath mountains in the reconstructed war.
Küyen’s selection as Antü’s wife motivates stars joining Peripillán’s rebellion.

Pillanes.note: Some later stories describe pillanes as Kai-Kai’s assistants.
Some later stories make Kai-Kai a descendant or child of pillanes.

Pu-am.note: A poorly sourced popular synthesis says Pu-am created the ngen.

Puma.note: Elal fights and subdues Puma while bringing dangerous animals under his authority.
Puma hunts a guanaco with Elal before refusing the human use of fire.

Püllü/am of the dead.myth: Manipulation of a vulnerable dead spirit
Püllü/am of the dead.note: A kalku may allegedly capture or manipulate the spirit of a deceased person.

Quetrupillán.note: Recent local narratives describe combat between Rukapillan and Quetrupillán.

Sintalk’n.note: The powerful warrior fights Elal and is defeated and imprisoned.
After defeating and imprisoning Sintalk’n, Elal devours him.

Sirena.note: Contemporary Chiloé classification identifies Sirena as the owner of fish.

Sirena Chilota.myth: Sirena Chilota helps carry the drowned aboard
Sirena Chilota.note: She assists Pincoya and Pincoy in conveying drowned mariners to the vessel.
Late genealogies make Sirena Chilota Millalobo's youngest daughter.
Sirena Chilota helps Millalobo within his organized marine kingdom.
Some recent summaries call Sirena his wife, conflicting with her usual daughter role.

Skunk.note: Elal takes the fire that Skunk falsely denies possessing.
Skunk receives or retains foul smell and degraded food after withholding fire.

Swan.note: Lista describes Swan among Elal’s swan brothers.
The strongest Swan carries bird-transformed Elal eastward across the sea.
Later versions have Swan carry infant Elal westward from an eastern island.

Taita Huenteyao.note: Williche tradition describes Huenteyao as a powerful coastal ngen at Pucatrihue.

Taita Wenteyao.note: Huilliche rites invoke Ngünechen and Wenteyao together, with Wenteyao serving as ancestral intercessor or territorial power.

Teo.note: Teo is Elal’s biological mother in the later Cloud Woman genealogy.

Terrible Guanaco.note: Elal kills the trial-animal by arrow or after trapping it in a bog.

The Thrauca.note: She is the Trauco’s female counterpart and carries a sexual dream omen.

Tkaur.note: Tkaur appears as a transformed or alternative name of Nóshtex; the identity is uncertain.

Tren-Tren.note: Kai-Kai raises the sea while Tren-Tren raises its mountain to protect refugees.
Tren-Tren.source: Rosales, Historia general, book I, chapter 1

Treng Treng.note: Küyen and Antü precede and create or govern the saving serpent.

Trengtreng.note: Antü and Küyen precede Trengtreng's flood struggle in some Neuquén accounts.
The reconstructed cycle makes Trengtreng the transformed son of Antü.
Antü's rebellious son is transformed into the serpent Trengtreng.

Trentren.note: Later accounts associate Ngünechen's protection with beneficial Trentren during the flood.
Pillan aids the inundating side while Trentren protects the survivors.

Térguerr.note: Later variants describe the rodent rescuer as Elal’s maternal grandmother.
She saves the infant, hides him underground, and raises him in her burrow.
She teaches Elal about plant food and routes through the mountains.

Unnamed primordial great serpent.myth: Great serpent shattered during a lunar cosmic catastrophe
Unnamed primordial great serpent.note: Individual Piwichen arise from fragments of the shattered primordial serpent.

Vaca Marina.note: Modern hierarchical accounts list Vaca Marina as a dangerous being under his sovereignty.

Vaca Marina Chilota.note: A late popular account says Camahueto reaches the sea to mate with her.

Virgin Mary.note: A machi closely identifies or associates Mary with the Moon.
Virgin Mary.source: Bacigalupo, Shamans of the Foye Tree

Virgin Mary.note: Some Capuchin teaching analogizes Mary with Ngünechen's Kushe or Ñuke aspect.
Virgin Mary.source: Foerster, Introducción a la religiosidad mapuche

Wangülen.note: The reconstructed war says Antü dims the rebellious Wangülen.
Late accounts call Küyen mother or ruler of the star beings.
Modern syntheses classify Küyen as the principal Wangülen.
Jealous stars rebel after Antü chooses Küyen as his preferred wife.
Modern summaries describe Wangülen as female companions or counterparts of pillanes.

Wangülén.note: Wangülén appears as a younger celestial member of Ngünechen's sacred family.

Weche Wentru.note: The young man accompanies Antü's senior forms as a younger member or aspect.

Wekufü.note: Later scholarship variously classifies Anchimallén as a Wekufü-type harmful power or comparable auxiliary.
Later authors classify the Chonchón as a wekufü, though sources remain inconsistent.
Modern pantheon charts classify Kai-Kai among destructive wekufü.

Wekufü.myth: Filew empowers healing against harmful wekufü possession
Wekufü.note: Filew enables the machi to identify, negotiate with, or expel harmful wekufü.
Wekufü.source: Foerster, Introducción a la religiosidad mapuche

Wekufü.note: Some accounts say an angered Ngünechen permits or commands wekufü to afflict people.
Núñez classifies Trauco among hostile forces described as wekufü or wedake newen.

Wenu Püllüam.note: This ancestral heavenly power was possibly generalized into the supreme Ngünechen complex.

Wenu püllüam.myth: Filew belongs to the ancestral upper-world spirit complex
Wenu püllüam.note: Filew is associated with ancestral sky spirits and may arrive from wenu mapu.

Wenumapu Fucha.note: Central Araucanian systems use this elder celestial figure as Antü Fucha's structural equivalent.

Wenumapu Kuse.note: Central Araucanian systems use this elder celestial figure as Antü Kuse's structural equivalent.

Witranalwe.myth: Spectral being exploited by harmful specialists
Witranalwe.note: Kalku are regionally associated with or said to exploit this dangerous nocturnal being.

Yepü.note: Yepü appears as a younger celestial member of Ngünechen's sacred family.

cave serpent.note: Anchimalguén guards a cave associated with a great serpent.

creator.note: The creator fashions Tren-Tren from special clay and orders it to warn humanity.

fish-kings.note: Fish-kings consume portions of the child offered to appease the sea powers.
fish-kings.source: Rosales, Historia general, book I, chapter 1

mermaids.note: Mermaids consume portions of the child cast into the sea as an offering.
mermaids.source: Rosales, Historia general, book I, chapter 1

the substituted servant.note: The servant wears the daughter’s clothes and name, but Elal recognizes the substitution.

Ñuke Küyen.note: Ñuke Küyen corresponds to Ngünechen's elder female heavenly aspect in some Huilliche schemes.

Ñuke Papai.note: With Füta Chachai, makes the world and appoints ngen as caretakers.

Ülcha Domo.note: The young woman accompanies Antü's senior forms as a younger member or aspect.
